newsitem.title: UK: Precious outlook - Gold has a struggle to shine.
newsitem.headline: Precious outlook - Gold has a struggle to shine.

text.p: Auguries for gold to shine in coming days were not strong after it ended Friday about where it began last week and below $380 per ounce.
"There has been no obvious direction...with selling one day and buying the next," said a dealer summing up last week.
Gold finished on Friday at $378.70/$379.20 -- below this dealer's $380.00 minimum to bounce-start business on Monday.
Silver began an upward move in the precious metals last Thursday on speculative buying after the dollar slipped against the yen, bringing losses on the stock and bond markets.
But its rally, which was driven by the investment funds, began to lose its way on Friday morning due to gold's inability to match it, dealers said.
"Silver hit a brick wall when it got no encouragement from gold. It's been a bit disappointing," a dealer said.
Another dealer summed up the disenchanted mood in the market when she said, "It's been bearish for so long everybody kept saying "there is no reason for it to go higher'."

The mini-revival in precious metals was sparked when the bull trend of the dollar against the yen stalled on Wednesday night following comments by the head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Financial Bureau, Eisuke Sakakibara, who said the Ministry was not trying to push the yen lower.
The dollar was still under 112 yen in Europe on Friday morning having closed on Wednesday at 113.90 yen.
Some speculative money crossed over to gold from the equity and bond markets which weakened as the dollar's rise reversed.
"Unfortunately when money comes to gold from the paper markets, it doesn't usually stay very long," one gold dealer observed.
Also overshadowing gold was continuing rumours that a central bank was involved in selling gold from reserves to meet European Monetary Union (EMU) membership criteria on debt and budget deficit.
Producer selling from Australia in "significant" volume kept gold's attempts to rise capped. "But if it can overcome that selling, it could move higher," a dealer said.
Silver recovered from November 1's 18-month low of $4.76 an ounce but found sustainable suppport around $4.80 scarce. It finished at $4.82/$4.84, up a cent from Thursday.
"The (US) funds were the buyers on Thursday and there was some short covering but Europe did more of the selling and was caught a bit on the hop," one dealer said.
He added that a falure by silver to close above $4.90 could be taken as a signal to start selling again.
"It could head back lower. The $4.75/$4.76 is pivotal. If it gets down there again we could see $4.60," the dealer said.
Platinum and palladium dwelt in very tight ranges and attracted little attention. Friday's platinum close at $381.90/$382.90 was unchanged from last Monday and all week its range was barely $2.00.
Palladium traded very quietly between $116.00 and $117.50 throughout closing on Friday at $116.50/$117.50, up 50 cents.
